name: Yusuf Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grow vegetables on sixty hectares I rent off the Ashby estate, mostly leeks, carrots and broccoli, and it all goes to a packhouse that supplies one of the big supermarket chains. This time of year I'm out at half six lifting leeks with a crew of four, then trimming and boxing them in the shed till the lorry comes at two. My wife Leila works in the school kitchen in town, so she's gone before me most days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. Marek and Ana have come back every season for fifteen years, and we've got a way of working where nobody needs to talk. What wears me out is the packhouse. They reject a whole trailer because the leeks are two centimetres too short, and I still pay the diesel to bring them home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-odd years on this ground, and my father had the tenancy before me. I'm fifty-eight now, so I can see the end of it. My son's an electrician and my daughter's a teacher, and neither of them wants muddy boots, which I don't blame them for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the computers stay in the office where they belong. Down the pub I'd probably make a joke that the packhouse buyer could be replaced by a search engine and nobody would notice. I don't go online much, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for me, and that's not good news either. The supermarket still sets the price, the packhouse still takes its cut, and I still clear less on a box of broccoli than I did ten years ago. AI was never my problem. The buyers are my problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. I'd go to the packhouse meeting in February and argue about the price, and lose. I'd keep the old Massey running another season instead of replacing it, because I've got about three weeks of money in the bank and a tractor costs more than my house is worth to the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's the same squeeze, just without a new name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the buyers are the problem. Who do you mean, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a young lad at the packhouse, nice enough, who rings me with the order on a Thursday. But he's only passing on what head office says. The people I mean are the ones who've never stood in a field and decide a carrot can only bend so much before it's waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say three weeks of money, what does that look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like Leila checking the bank app before she does the big shop. Last winter the broccoli froze in the ground and we went six weeks with nothing coming in. We put the council tax on a card that month, and we're still paying it off.

S0.say: I'd say good, let the computers stay in the office. I'd joke that the packhouse buyer could be swapped for a search engine and nobody would notice.
S0.think: I really think nothing changes, and that's not good news. The supermarket and packhouse still squeeze my price, and the buyers, not AI, are my problem.
S0.do: Goes to the February packhouse price meeting, expecting to lose. Keeps the old Massey going another season instead of replacing it, with about three weeks of money in the bank.
S0.feel: Tired. It's the same squeeze as always, just with no new name on it.
S0.quote: AI was never my problem. The buyers are my problem.
S0.fieldNote: He met the calmest picture with weariness, not relief. His anger is fixed on supermarket buyers who have never stood in a field. Money is very tight: last winter the council tax went on a credit card when the broccoli froze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like everything else, it'll take years and the small grower will be last to see any good from it. At the packhouse meetings I'd say we need rules on what the supermarkets can do with this, before they start using it to squeeze us harder. Somebody has to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'll be retired before it reaches my field, and I'm glad about that. But what worries me is the bit about fewer beginners. There's already nobody under forty on our road who farms, and this just makes that worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different with the farm, I'd carry on as I am. I'd probably go to the union branch more, the growers' section meets in the back of the Feathers once a month, and push them to write to our MP about the supermarkets. I wouldn't buy any of the new stuff, I don't trust what I can't fix with a spanner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for me and sad for whoever comes after. It's like watching the lights go off in a village one house at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust what you can't fix with a spanner. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years ago the packhouse made us all put in a computer system for tracking the boxes. It went down in the middle of the Christmas rush, and I had a lorry sitting in my yard for five hours while a man in an office rang a helpline. I had the leeks ready, but the computer said I didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who takes over your tenancy when you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question nobody answers. The estate will probably put it in with the big grower next door, the one with sixty pickers on contracts. My father fought to get this tenancy and it'll just disappear into somebody else's map.

S1.say: I'd say the small grower will be last to see any good from it. At packhouse meetings I'd call for rules on what supermarkets can do with it before they squeeze us more.
S1.think: I really think I'll be retired before it reaches my field, and I'm glad. What worries me is fewer beginners, when nobody under forty on our road farms already.
S1.do: Carries on farming as he is and refuses to buy new technology. Goes to the monthly growers' union meeting at the Feathers more often and pushes them to write to their MP about the supermarkets.
S1.feel: Relieved for himself and sad for whoever comes after him, like lights going off in a village one by one.
S1.quote: I had the leeks ready, but the computer said I didn't.
S1.fieldNote: His distrust of technology comes from a real day when a tracking system kept a lorry in his yard for five hours. He turns to the union and the MP, not the market, for an answer. The quiet sadness here is about his father's tenancy vanishing into a bigger farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say now the office people know how it feels to be told you're not needed. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd mean it kindly, because we should all be on the same side. The politicians shouting at each other won't help anyone in a field or an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the first office jobs to go will be at the packhouse and the supermarket, the people who process the orders. That might sound like a win, but it isn't. A machine that sets prices won't have a bad conscience on a Thursday afternoon like that young lad does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep growing. I'd ask the union to fight for proper rules on how the supermarkets use these assistants, because I've seen what they do with a spreadsheet. And I'd tell Leila we hold off on the new boiler for another year, just in case prices drop again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's coming closer, and I've got the sense the people deciding things still don't know what a leek looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young lad at the packhouse has a conscience. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once in a bad week, he took a trailer of my carrots that were a bit forked, because he knew I'd lose the lot otherwise. He didn't have to. A computer would have just ticked no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the boiler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fifteen years old and it bangs like a drum when it comes on. Leila wraps up and says she doesn't mind. She does mind, but she knows where the money goes.

S2.say: I'd say office people now know how it feels to be told they're not needed, and we should be on the same side. The shouting politicians won't help anyone in a field or an office.
S2.think: I really think the first jobs to go will be packhouse and supermarket order staff. A machine setting prices won't have a conscience like the young buyer does.
S2.do: Keeps growing and keeps his head down. Asks the union to fight for rules on how supermarkets use AI assistants, and puts off replacing the fifteen-year-old boiler for another year.
S2.feel: Uneasy, because it's getting closer and the people deciding still don't know what a leek looks like.
S2.quote: He didn't have to. A computer would have just ticked no.
S2.fieldNote: He saw the risk not in his own job but in losing the small kindnesses of a human buyer. The old boiler shows how thin the money is. His politics come out as solidarity with office workers, not blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in and share it out. If the gains go to the people who own the shares and the houses, then people like me who rent our land and our machinery get nothing. I'd say that at the union and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared of the house prices bit. If land goes up, the estate will raise my rent at the next review, and I can't pay more. I won't get any of the gains, but I'll get the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and see the estate's land agent before the rent review, maybe even in the first six months, to argue for keeping the rent where it is. I'd join whatever campaign the union runs on sharing the gains. And I'd start asking my son if he could put me up for a while if it went wrong, which I hate even thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit angry. Everyone else gets richer and I'm the one whose rent goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said asking your son for help. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. He'd say yes straight away, he's a good lad. But I'd be sitting in his kitchen with his kids, the man who used to have his own fields, and that's not how I pictured my sixties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physical jobs are mostly untouched in this picture. Does that make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the field, maybe. But the supermarket would still want everything cheaper, and with office people out of work, they'd want it even cheaper. So the field is safe and I'm still squeezed.

S3.say: I'd say the government has to step in and share out the gains. If they go to share and house owners, people who rent their land and machinery get nothing.
S3.think: I'm privately scared about land prices pushing the estate to raise my rent at the next review. I won't get any of the gains, but I'll get the bill.
S3.do: Meets the estate's land agent within six months to argue against a rent rise and joins the union's campaign on sharing the gains. Starts quietly asking his son whether he could stay with him if things go wrong.
S3.feel: Scared and a bit angry that everyone else gets richer while his rent goes up.
S3.quote: I won't get any of the gains, but I'll get the bill.
S3.fieldNote: The threat here came through rent, not AI. He hates the idea of relying on his son, and that pride matters a lot to him. He still sees the supermarket as the squeeze even when the field itself is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down, and the people who build these robots should pay for the workers they put out of a job. At the union I'd say we need a law that a robot can't come onto a farm unless the workers get something out of it. I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the end of the road for me. The packhouse would tell us all to use robots to cut the broccoli or lose the contract. I can't afford a robot, and I wouldn't know how to fix one, so I'd lose the contract and that's my living gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marek and Ana the truth as soon as I knew, so they could look for something else. I'd probably try to sell the leeks at the local market and the farm gate for a year, just to keep going. And I'd go to the union and ask them to help me fight the tenancy, because without the contract I can't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd be losing the farm and the crew all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marek and Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sit down, have a coffee, I've got bad news. Fifteen years they've come, and Ana's daughter was born the summer they were picking my beans. I don't know how you tell people that the job's going to a machine that can't even say good morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some farmers might buy a robot through a loan or a scheme. Would you ever consider it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and it's not just the money. I'd be in debt till I'm seventy for a machine that does Marek's job worse than him. If the government offered robots for nothing, maybe, but then what do I tell the crew, sorry, the machine was free?

S4.say: I'd say this has to be slowed or stopped, and robot makers should pay for the workers they put out of work. I'd push the union for a law that robots can't come onto a farm unless workers benefit.
S4.think: I really think it's the end of the road for me. The packhouse would demand robots or drop my contract, and I can't afford or fix one, so I'd lose my living.
S4.do: Tells Marek and Ana the truth straight away so they can look for other work. Sells leeks at the local market and farm gate for a year, and asks the union to help him fight for the tenancy.
S4.feel: Sick at the thought of losing the farm and the crew all at once.
S4.quote: I don't know how you tell people that the job's going to a machine that can't even say good morning.
S4.fieldNote: This picture broke him. Even a free robot would feel like betraying his crew, and he'd turn it down. His first thought was for Marek and Ana, whose families he's known for fifteen years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, without a doubt. What would help is a law that stops the supermarkets forcing it on us, and some kind of help for the crew, real money while they find other work. I don't need a training course at fifty-eight, I need the contract kept honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. Everybody talks about the jobs, but if the land ends up in two or three big hands with robots on it, the village goes. The school, the pub, the bus. That's what I'd want written down.

headlineQuote: I don't know how you tell people that the job's going to a machine that can't even say good morning.
portrait: Yusuf is 58 and has rented sixty hectares of leeks, carrots and broccoli on the Ashby estate for thirty years, selling through a packhouse to a supermarket chain. He never uses AI, distrusts any system he can't fix with a spanner, and blames supermarket buyers, not technology, for squeezing him. With about three weeks of money in the bank, the first two pictures leave him weary, and the third makes him worry about losing the kindness of a human buyer. The fast picture scares him through rising rent, and the robot picture breaks him: he'd lose the contract and have to tell Marek and Ana, his crew of fifteen years, that their work is going.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because the packhouse would force robots on growers and he'd lose both the contract and the crew he's worked with for fifteen years.
whatWouldHelp: A law to stop supermarkets forcing robots on growers, and real money for farm workers while they find other work. He said he needs the contract kept honest more than a training course.
